title: 1.2. Introduction to Python & Evolution
summary: Discover the origins of Python by Guido van Rossum, the philosophy behind The Zen of Python, and the crucial distinction between compilation and interpretation.
learningObjectives: Trace the historical development of Python and Guido van Rossum's guiding design principles.
Compare compiled languages (C, C++, Rust) with interpreted languages (Python, JavaScript).
Understand the CPython runtime pipeline: source code (.py) -> bytecode (.pyc) -> Python Virtual Machine (PVM).

sections.heading: 1.2.1 The Birth and Philosophy of Python
sections.content:
Python was conceived in the late 1980s by Dutch programmer Guido van Rossum at CWI (Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica) in Amsterdam. It was officially released to the public in 1991.

Van Rossum named the language after the British comedy series 'Monty Python's Flying Circus', reflecting a desire to make programming enjoyable and accessible rather than dry and intimidating.

The core design tenets of Python are formalized in PEP 20 — 'The Zen of Python' (written by Tim Peters):
• Beautiful is better than ugly.
• Explicit is better than implicit.
• Simple is better than complex.
• Readability counts.

sections.heading: 1.2.2 Compilation vs. Interpretation: The CPython Pipeline
sections.content:
How does Python execute your source code?

1. Source Code (.py): You author clean textual instructions.
2. CPython Compiler: When you run python script.py, the interpreter first compiles your high-level code into platform-independent intermediate instructions called bytecode (.pyc).
3. Python Virtual Machine (PVM): The PVM reads each bytecode instruction, translates it on the fly into host CPU machine instructions, and coordinates memory management.

This hybrid model provides rapid development cycles, cross-platform portability, and powerful dynamic features.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Who created the Python programming language?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Guido van Rossum invented Python and served as its Benevolent Dictator for Life (BDFL) until 2018.

recap: Python is an interpreted, bytecode-executed language designed for human readability and productivity.
